---
title: "Wildfire policy begins before the fire"
description: "Europe is treating wildfire less as an emergency event and more as a land-management problem. Ireland has reasons to pay attention."
date: 2026-09-24
categories: ["Policy", "Land & Agriculture"]
draft: true
---

A wildfire is most visible when the flames arrive. Policy has usually arrived much earlier, whether anyone notices it or not.

The condition of an upland before a dry spell, the amount of combustible vegetation, whether grazing continues, how forests are managed, where access routes and water points sit, and whether neighbouring land managers cooperate all shape what happens when ignition occurs. That makes wildfire an emergency-management problem, but not only an emergency-management problem. It is also a question of how landscapes are managed between fires.

The European Commission moved further in that direction on 25 March 2026 when it adopted a Communication on Integrated Wildfire Risk Management. The Commission's [guidance for agriculture and forests](https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/cap-my-country/sustainability/environmental-sustainability/wildfire-prevention-and-restoration-agriculture-and-forests_en) treats prevention, preparedness, response and recovery as parts of the same system. Farmers and foresters appear throughout that cycle. Grazing, agroforestry, thinning, firebreaks and other forms of active management can reduce fuel accumulation and help maintain more varied landscapes. After a fire, land managers also become part of restoration.

Ireland is not Mediterranean Europe, and importing a southern European fire narrative would be misleading. Its risk profile is different. Yet the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine's [fire-management guidance](https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-agriculture-food-and-the-marine/publications/fire-management/) identifies dry spring conditions as a vulnerable period and notes how readily gorse, dead vegetation and other fuels can burn. The same page records several Fire Danger Notices during 2026. The Office of Emergency Planning also identifies peatlands, turf-cutting bogs, uplands and immature forest lands among the places most prone to wildfire in Ireland.

The policy question, then, is not whether Ireland is becoming Spain or Greece. It is how much wildfire policy should concern itself with the ordinary management of rural landscapes.

There is already evidence of that logic in Irish guidance. Forest owners are advised to maintain firebreaks, prepare access routes and water sources, develop fire plans and cooperate with neighbouring landowners. [Teagasc's guidance for forest owners](https://teagasc.ie/crops/forestry/advice/management/dealing-with-wildfires/) makes the same point about firebreaks, planning and cooperation. The [Office of Emergency Planning](https://www.gov.ie/en/office-of-emergency-planning/guidance/wildfires/) notes that active farming, appropriate livestock grazing and other fuel-reduction measures can reduce fire risk. These are mundane interventions compared with aircraft and fire engines. Their importance lies precisely in occurring before an emergency.

This creates a familiar policy difficulty. Landscape management produces benefits that do not stop at a property boundary. A grazed or well-managed parcel may reduce fuel in a wider area. A blocked access route or unmanaged strip may increase risk beyond the holding on which it sits. Prevention therefore has a coordination problem similar to those found in biodiversity, water quality and invasive-species management.

The European approach is useful because it widens the unit of analysis. The farm or forest remains important, but so do mosaics of land uses, neighbouring holdings and the connections between them. That does not mean every landscape should be intensively managed. Peatlands and habitats have ecological objectives that can conflict with poorly designed interventions, and prescribed burning itself requires expertise, legal compliance and careful timing. Prevention cannot become a justification for indiscriminate vegetation removal.

There is another caution. It is easy to infer effectiveness from a plausible mechanism. Grazing can reduce some fuels, for example, but the effect depends on stocking, vegetation, season, terrain and the ecological system being protected. The useful question is where an intervention works, at what intensity, at what cost, and with what consequences for biodiversity, carbon and farming.

By the time a hillside is burning, many of the variables that shape the event have already been set. That is why wildfire increasingly belongs in conversations about land management as well as emergency response.

For Ireland, the lesson from Europe's current approach is fairly modest: fire policy begins with the landscape long before it begins with the flame.
